query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, the simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion is governed by the formation of an adaptive dual-layer at the surface: a mechanically robust, passivating oxide film that self-heals during wear, together with a refined, ultra-nanocrystalline subsurface microstructure that accommodates deformation. This dual-layer structure minimizes material removal and retards corrosive attack compared to conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNiMo-based composition) with a chemically disordered, multi-principal element microstructure in its as-synthesized state.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled thermal/oxidation treatment designed to promote the in situ formation of a dense, protective oxide film and to induce surface grain refinement (via dynamic recrystallization or controlled annealing), in one set of samples, while leaving a matched set untreated.
generation.conditions: Testing in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under mechanical wear conditions such as sliding contact or tribocorrosion tests at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense passivating oxide layer (e.g., rich in Mo- or Ti-oxides) coupled with an ultra-nanocrystalline subsurface structure that forms dynamically under wear, serving as a mechanical buffer.
generation.mechanism: The passivating oxide film prevents or slows down electrochemical attack, while the refined subsurface microstructure – generated or maintained by controlled thermal treatment – enhances wear resistance by accommodating deformation and reducing the tendency for crack initiation. This synergistic interaction lowers both wear rates and corrosion current densities in the service environment.
generation.predicted_outcome: The thermally treated high-entropy alloy will exhibit lower friction coefficients and wear rates as well as lower corrosion current densities and more stable corrosion potentials compared to the untreated baseline. The dual-layer is expected to sustain performance during combined tribocorrosion tests.
generation.baseline: A matched high-entropy alloy sample in its as-synthesized (untreated) state that lacks the engineered dual-layer surface structure.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds when the alloy composition is capable of forming robust oxides (e.g., through adequate Mo, Ti, or similar elements) and when processing conditions allow grain refinement. The effect may not be observable in alloys with compositions that cannot form stable passivating layers or when operating under conditions (extreme temperatures, excessive mechanical loads) that disrupt the dual-layer structure.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative synergistic effect is supported by prior evidence, the precise magnitude of improvements in wear and corrosion resistance and the relative contributions of the oxide film versus the refined microstructure remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical bulk compositions. Subject one set to a controlled thermal treatment to induce the formation of the passivating oxide film and subsurface grain refinement, while keeping the other set untreated. Expose both sets to simultaneous wear and corrosion testing (e.g., tribocorrosion tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under controlled sliding conditions) and monitor performance over time.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., mm³/N·m) via mass loss or profilometry
Electrochemical measurements (corrosion potential, corrosion current density)
Surface and subsurface microstructural characterization (SEM/EDS, XRD) to verify oxide layer and grain refinement
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both wear resistance and corrosion metrics (i.e., similar or worse performance compared to the untreated samples), or if the expected dual-layer microstructure is absent despite treatment, then the hypothesis that the adaptive dual-layer governs combined degradation resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

This study demonstrates that the proposed alloy design delivers substantial improvements in both wear and corrosion resistance. The work clarifies how boron doping modifies the microstructure, establishes the linkage between microstructural features and performance, and derives general design principles for engineering coatings. We define this strategy as a generalized methodology for coating performance enhancement. While the present study does not address specific service environments, machinability, or long-term stability, we contend that with its robust performance foundation, the coating can be further optimized through compositional tuning and post-processing to enable reliable service across a broad range of applications.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
